results.title: Estimating the Complier Average Causal Effect in a Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials With Binary Outcomes Accounting for Noncompliance: A Generalized Linear Latent and Mixed Model Approach - PMC
results.content: # Estimating the Complier Average Causal Effect in a Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials With Binary Outcomes Accounting for Noncompliance: A Generalized Linear Latent and Mixed Model Approach. **Keywords:** complier average causal effect, generalized linear latent and mixed model, meta-analysis, noncompliance, randomized clinical trials. Thus, this article describes in detail a closely related frequentist approach analogous to the BHM, the generalized linear latent and mixed models (GLLAMMs), using exactly the same model specification to estimate the CACE in a meta-analysis of RCTs accounting for noncompliance, in the widely used SAS (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, North Carolina) system. Compared with a 2-step meta-analysis, which computes study-specific CACE estimates and their standard errors first, then uses either a fixed or random effects model to produce a weighted average (17), GLLAMMs use an exact binomial likelihood and do not depend on an asymptotic approximation for study-specific estimates. We then compared the CACE estimated from the GLLAMM with that from BHM and ITT analysis in a meta-analysis of the effect of epidural analgesia in labor on the cesarean delivery. Figure 2 presents the forest plot of effect estimates for the case study comparing the study-specific risk difference (RD) using ITT analysis and a “2-step” approach with either the BHM as presented in Zhou et al. Estimated Probability of Selecting the True Random-Effects Model Based on 1,000 Simulated Data Sets (Number of Studies = 20, per-Study Sample Size = 350). To our knowledge, this is the first paper to propose a GLLAMM approach to estimating the CACE in a meta-analysis of RCTs, accounting for various heterogeneities between studies in noncompliance and treatment effects using random effects. As the case study and simulations show, the GLLAMMs allow us to build a class of random-effects models with different complexities to account for various between-study heterogeneity structures, which are common in a meta-analysis. Therefore, more theoretical and methodological work is needed to better understand how to define the target population and to estimate causal effects in a meta-analysis when the population of compliers varies substantially across trials, particularly when the study-specific CACEs are heterogeneous. results.title: Beyond intent to treat (ITT): A complier average causal effect (CACE) estimation primer - ScienceDirect
results.content: Randomized control trials (RCTs) have long been the gold standard for allowing causal inferences to be made regarding the efficacy of a treatment under investigation, but traditional RCT data analysis perspectives do not take into account a common reality: imperfect participant compliance to treatment. Recent advances in both maximum likelihood parameter estimation and mixture modeling methodology have enabled treatment effects to be estimated, in the presence of less than ideal levels of participant compliance, via a Complier Average Causal Effect (CACE) structural equation mixture model. CACE model assumptions, specification, estimation, and interpretation will all be demonstrated with simulated data generated from a randomized controlled trial of cognitive-behavioral therapy for Juvenile Fibromyalgia. First, the simulated JFM RCT data were analyzed with a longitudinal SEM intent to treat (ITT) analysis, first with no covariates (an unconditional model), then with the inclusion of age, depression, pain severity and group (a conditional model). First, prior to removing the exclusion restriction and examining the change (if any) on the CACE treatment effect estimate as a result of adding additional covariates, we estimate a conditional *ITT* model to establish a comparison baseline. Results for the conditional ITT model illustrated in Fig. 7 showed that participants had an FDI score of 18.87 (*α*0 = 18.65, *p* < .001) at the start of the study, and control group. Taken together, results from all CACE analysis models suggest that a participant randomly assigned to the CBT treatment group, and found to be compliant with the treatment regimen, will tend to experience greater decreases in FDI scores over time versus a participant randomly assigned to the CBT treatment group but found to be non-compliant. ### Estimating psychological treatment effects from a randomized controlled trial with both non-compliance and loss to follow-up. * ### A task-shared, collaborative care psychosocial intervention for improving depressive symptomatology among older adults in a socioeconomically deprived area of Brazil (PROACTIVE): a pragmatic, two-arm, parallel-group, cluster-randomised controlled trial. We identified 24 primary care clinics in Guarulhos that were willing to participate, of which 20 were randomly allocated to either the control group (ten [50%] clusters) or to the intervention group (ten [50%] clusters).

results.title: Estimating intervention effects of prevention programs: Accounting for noncompliance - PMC
results.content: Estimating the effect of fully participating (known as the complier average causal effect [CACE]) as well as the effect of being assigned to the treatment group (known as the intent to treat [ITT] effect) allows researchers to obtain a more complete view of the effects of their interventions. In both studies, there is interest in estimating not just the effect of being assigned to the intervention group, but also the effect of actually participating in most of the intervention activities. Unfortunately this method also yields biased estimates of the effects, since it conditions on just the observed participation levels and implicitly compares individuals in the treatment and control groups with the same observed participation (Frangakis & Rubin, 2002). Because individuals are assigned to the treatment and control groups randomly in experimental evaluations, we can easily obtain an unbiased estimate of the ITT effect by comparing the average outcomes in the treatment and control groups. The challenge in estimating the CACE arises because participation is not randomly assigned and we observe each individual in either the treatment group or the control group—never both. These assumptions are briefly restated: 1) The outcomes of one individual are not affected by the treatment assignments of any other individuals (SUTVA); 2) The opportunity to participate was assigned randomly; 3) There are some compliers; 4) There are no defiers (monotonicity); and, 5) There is no effect of assignment for the always-takers or the never-taker (the exclusion restrictions). A promising approach could be to use latent class analysis among treatment group members to identify different participation classes (e.g., as in Lin, Ten Have, & Elliott, in press), and then use those as the levels of compliance when estimating the CACE, but that approach has not been systematically examined. As an alternative to the CACE models described here, another approach sometimes used to estimate the effects of levels of participation is propensity score matching, where individuals in the treatment group with some participation level are matched to individuals in the control group with similar baseline characteristics (Foster, 2003; Hill, Brooks-Gunn, & Waldfogel, 2003).
